title: The Ninth Photograph
setting: An island radio station holding an old rescue review
anchor: the original distress reel and an uncropped rescue photograph
pressure: A recorded voice and an uncropped photograph could overturn the account of a lost trawler. Someone has killed to keep them apart.
opening: At 21:17 Abel Rook speaks over the station loudspeaker, asking for a tow for a trawler lost thirteen years ago. In the transmitter room you find Rook dead beside a tape deck. On his desk is a rescue photograph you know from the newspapers, but this print is wider: at its edge a small patched launch lies below the island slip. You came to witness his account of the wreck. Now the voice and the photograph must speak without him.

The relief boat cannot cross the rising sea. Six people remain at the station: its relief keeper and engineer, a rescue mechanic, a photographer, a nurse, and a drowned deckhand’s daughter. The organization behind the trawler’s final voyage has survived thirteen years of inquiries. One person here still works for it. Rook had invited the others to compare the distress reel with the uncropped rescue sequence, something the original inquiry never did.

Before the first watch, you collect signed accounts and place the reel and photograph on the chart-room table. Each witness has repeated an old version of that night often enough to mistake familiarity for certainty. Below the closed window, the island bell has already finished its nine strikes. You ask everyone to remember whether they heard it once, or twice.

cast.name: Mara
cast.description: Mara still wears the station keys on a cord inside her sweater. Rook trained her, then refused to retire fully.
cast.relationship: She shares the night watches with Elias and resents his habit of correcting her logs.
cast.account: I was winding the bell mechanism at 21:00. I wrote down nine strikes, then carried the winding handle upstairs. I heard Rook’s voice later, after I had reached the chart room.
cast.observation: The bell runs on a weight, not the station battery. It keeps ringing when the lights fail. The chart-room window was shut tonight; from there, nine strikes sound like one long rattling noise.
cast.secret: I put my name on two of Rook’s shifts last winter. He was losing track of dates and I wanted to keep him employed. My handwriting in his log does not mean I made his recordings.
cast.defense: Check the winding handle. It stays with me until the mechanism is locked. I can account for a bell; I cannot account for a man behind a closed door.
cast.correction: I recorded the bell when I finished winding, not when I first entered the tower. My nine-strike note anchors that sound; it does not account for every minute I spent on the stairs.

cast.name: Elias
cast.description: Elias has brought a small repair case and a larger overnight bag. He offers to restore the transmitter before anyone asks.
cast.relationship: He maintains the station and helped collect the company’s witness statements after the old wreck.
cast.account: At 21:00 I was on the roof, changing the antenna coupling. I came down when the loudspeaker came on at 21:17. I never touched that tape. On the night of the wreck I stayed at the station; I never used the little launch.
cast.observation: These decks pick up all kinds of background noise. Wind can sound remarkably like a bell when you listen for it. I would be careful about promising a bereaved family an answer from a bad recording.
cast.secret: The shipping company kept paying me as a maintenance consultant after the wreck. I should have declared that before this review. I also owe Rook money for repairs he says I billed but did not complete.
cast.defense: A maintenance signature gives me responsibility for a machine. It does not put me beside it every minute of the night.
cast.correction: I did come below for a fuse. Saying I stayed on the roof was too absolute. I still say that a repair journey does not establish that I handled Rook’s reel.

cast.name: Ivo
cast.description: Ivo keeps a wet cap folded between his hands. He served on the rescue vessel but has not spoken about that night in years.
cast.relationship: He repaired the white canvas patch on the company launch before the wreck and later served on the rescue vessel.
cast.account: I isolated the roof feed from 20:56 until 21:12. Elias had borrowed my long-handled coupling wrench at 20:50, saying he needed it upstairs. I stayed in the battery room with the isolation key.
cast.observation: When I called upstairs at 21:04, Elias answered through the workshop speaking tube. I could hear the little whistle the tube makes before it opens. The roof has a telephone, not a tube.
cast.secret: I drank on the rescue watch thirteen years ago. I remember the order to turn away, but not who repeated it. Rook wanted a certainty I could not give him.
cast.defense: I can show you the isolated circuit. What I cannot do is make thirteen years of missing memory return because you need it tonight.
cast.correction: I recognized the workshop tube before I recognized the voice. I am confident about where the answer came from; I cannot see through a tube and identify who else was in the room.

cast.name: Nell
cast.description: Nell lays out contact sheets instead of the photograph everyone recognizes. She keeps her finger off the small boat at the edge.
cast.relationship: She took the rescue photograph, then worked with Rook to compare its uncropped sequence with the distress reel.
cast.account: I showed Rook the uncropped sequence at 20:40. The frame before the famous photograph shows Elias beside the patched launch. Rook played the first few seconds of his old reel for me: two harbor whistles, with no bell underneath.
cast.observation: The message at 21:17 began with nine bell strikes under Rook’s voice. I recorded it from the chart room. The island bell itself had finished seventeen minutes earlier; I remember because we stopped talking to count it.
cast.secret: I accepted an award for the cropped rescue photograph without mentioning that the editor had removed the launch. By then I knew people were using my picture as proof that only one boat had reached the slip.
cast.defense: My recording has its own clock, and that clock may be wrong. Compare the sounds themselves before you use my timestamp.
cast.correction: The station clock dates the sequence only approximately. I should distinguish that from the order of frames, which the negative preserves. The bell in my recording is a separate check.

cast.name: Ada
cast.description: Ada has opened her first-aid bag but left the blanket folded. She knew Rook well enough to know which chair he would refuse.
cast.relationship: She treated survivors of the wreck and kept both her original notes and the corrected inquiry copy.
cast.account: I saw Rook alive at 20:48. He was waiting for someone to look at the deck. Afterward Sera and I were in the kitchen. We both heard the loudspeaker message; neither of us was with Rook when it began.
cast.observation: I kept my original rescue notes after correcting one arrival time for the inquiry. They put the patched launch at the slip before the first ambulance. I cannot identify its driver from that note alone.
cast.secret: I moved one patient’s recorded arrival time because I feared being blamed for a delay. I kept the earlier page. When Sera asked for it years later, I told her I had lost it.
cast.defense: I will give you the times I actually saw him. I will not dress a guess about his death in medical language.
cast.correction: My original rescue note records the launch before the ambulance. It does not record its arrival or its driver. I should not let a true early sighting become a complete journey.

cast.name: Sera
cast.description: Sera has brought a photograph in a supermarket envelope. She does not put it down beside the tape.
cast.relationship: Her father died on the trawler; Elias helped write her old statement, while Ada treated her on the slip.
cast.account: Ada and I were in the kitchen from just before nine. When the bell rang, I went for a dry cloth and saw Elias leaving the transmitter corridor with a small reel. I noticed the white patch on its edge.
cast.observation: The rescue statement I signed says only the lifeboat was present. Elias suggested that wording when he helped with the company forms. I had never seen the whole slip; I was repeating an answer he made sound settled.
cast.secret: I threatened Rook in a letter because he had kept the original reel for thirteen years. I also let that sentence about the lifeboat stand after I began doubting it. I was ashamed to reopen a statement with my own name on it.
cast.defense: I saw a reel and a man. Do not make me say I watched a murder when I did not.
cast.correction: I saw Elias leaving the corridor, not stepping through the transmitter-room door. The white reel is the detail I actually saw. The rest of that route must be checked against somebody else’s account.

connections.speaker: mara
connections.subject: elias
connections.text: Ivo heard you answer the workshop tube while your account puts you on the roof, Elias. The bell gives us a shared interval. You may have had a reason to come down, but that journey belongs in your statement.
connections.reply: I came below for a fuse. I should have said so. Coming down for a repair is not the same as entering the transmitter room.

connections.speaker: nell
connections.subject: elias
connections.text: The new leader and tonight’s bell belong to a replacement recording. Sera places you on its route. The photograph explains why making the original sound unreliable would matter to you: it puts you beside a boat you said you never used.
connections.reply: A photograph can show me beside a launch without showing what I did with it. You are using one disputed interval to decide another thirteen years earlier.

connections.speaker: ada
connections.subject: mara
connections.text: Mara’s false entries protected a man who was losing his memory. They require correction, but they do not supply the new reel or explain Elias’s omitted journey. We should not let the first admitted lie close the inquiry.
connections.reply: I will identify every shift I signed for him. Let the corrected pages stay beside the originals.

timeline: Thirteen years earlier, Elias used the company launch while the rescue account was being managed; Nell’s uncropped photographs and Ada’s original notes recorded its presence.
20:40 Rook and Nell compare the uncropped sequence with the old reel, whose opening contains two whistles.
20:48 Ada sees Rook alive; at 20:50 Elias borrows Ivo’s coupling wrench.
20:56 the roof feed is isolated. Elias goes to the transmitter room, strikes Rook with the wrench, and prepares a replacement reel.
21:00 the island bell rings nine times; Elias records it underneath the old voice. Sera sees him on the corridor route with the new reel.
21:04 Elias answers Ivo through the workshop tube, contradicting his uninterrupted roof alibi.
21:17 the replacement reel plays, creating the false appearance of a fresh message from Rook.
solution: Elias killed Rook with the borrowed coupling wrench and substituted a recording containing tonight’s bell beneath the old distress message. He needed the original to look like a recent reconstruction: paired with Nell’s wider photograph, it challenged the rescue account he had helped the shipping organization manage. The tube fixes his omitted journey; the fresh leader, Sera’s sighting, and the repeated bell connect him to the substitution. The photograph exposes the older lie without alone proving tonight’s murder.
chapters: A voice with no witness
The wider photograph lies beside the reel. You begin with what each object can establish, before allowing either one to explain the other.
The second version
The lower jetty is underwater. An old statement can be repeated perfectly and still contain a sentence nobody witnessed.
The edge of the picture
The harbor light becomes visible beyond the spray. The review must leave the island with its originals and its corrections together.
ending_win: The relief boat takes the reel and the full contact strip ashore in separate sealed cases. Sera asks for the two whistles to be played without commentary. Nell names the people at the edge of her photograph before anyone offers to crop it again.
ending_loss: The replacement reel is accepted as the station’s only authenticated recording. The photograph becomes an argument about clocks and perspective. Elias’s old version survives because the surviving objects are no longer allowed to explain each other.
reconstruction: Elias was the organization’s agent. Thirteen years earlier he had helped manage the account of the trawler’s failed rescue, using the small company launch while the public story excluded any second boat. Nell’s uncropped sequence and Ada’s original note preserved details that the published picture and corrected inquiry pages had hidden. Rook planned to make the old distress reel answer those independent records.

On the review night Elias borrowed Ivo’s coupling wrench and used the supposed roof repair to approach the transmitter room. After Ada’s last sighting of Rook, Elias struck him with the wrench. He prepared a replacement reel by recording the old voice together with the island’s nine o’clock bell. Playing it at 21:17 would make Rook appear to have just spoken and would let the company dismiss the old recording as a recent reconstruction.

Ivo’s speaking-tube observation breaks the uninterrupted roof alibi. Sera’s sighting places Elias on the route with the white-backed reel. The fresh leader and repeated bell explain the substitution. The photograph does not, by itself, prove tonight’s killing; it explains why discrediting the reel and controlling the rescue account mattered to Elias.

The others had helped silence the past in different ways. Nell accepted credit for a cropped picture, Ada edited an arrival time and withheld the original, and Sera repeated a statement Elias had supplied. Ivo concealed his drinking and the limits of his memory. Mara signed Rook’s shifts to keep him employed. Those failings made suspicion plausible, but none explains the newly made reel and Elias’s omitted journey.

title: A Room Kept Warm
setting: A hilltop hospice during an avalanche closure
pressure: The estate trustee is dead, and an unsigned transfer would move the hospice into a criminal holding company.
opening: Every empty room in Saint Orla’s is cold except Room Four. Its radiator ticks against a bed that has not been slept in for a week. You arrive to witness a patient’s amendment to the trust that owns the hospice. Instead, the estate trustee lies dead at the foot of the service stairs, one slipper missing. His briefcase is open. The amendment is gone.

The avalanche crossed the access road at dusk. Six people remain with you in the old wing: staff, a contractor, a relative, and the officer sent to complete the transfer. The remaining patients were evacuated that afternoon. By morning, an electronic signature could hand the property to a company the trustee had begun investigating. One person here needs the paper destroyed before anyone can compare it with the digital version.

You close the office, collect signed accounts, and organize watches from the dining room. Room Four stays warm. Nobody volunteers to turn its valve down. Somewhere inside the walls, a pipe knocks three times and falls quiet.

cast.name: Hana
cast.description: Hana has written the evacuated patients’ destinations on the back of a menu. She checks it whenever the lights dip.
cast.relationship: She knew the dying patient who made the amendment and challenged the proposed transfer.
cast.account: I left the trustee in the office at 18:20. He asked whether Room Four was still empty. I said yes. At 18:35 I was packing the last medical bag with Jules in the dining room.
cast.observation: Room Four’s heat was turned up after the evacuation. I had set it to frost protection myself. The service passage from that room reaches the office stairs without crossing the dining room.
cast.secret: The patient asked me to hide a copy of her amendment. I refused because I thought the signed original was safe with the trustee. I keep thinking that a small breach of procedure might have saved him.
cast.defense: The passage is no secret. I can tell you who uses it at work, but that is not the same as telling you who used it tonight.
cast.correction: I saw the trustee in the office at 18:20. My later time comes from Jules’s kitchen clock. I can stand by the order of those visits more firmly than the exact ten-minute interval.

cast.name: Leonie
cast.description: Leonie has set out signature tabs on a dry napkin. Even now she aligns their corners before answering.
cast.relationship: She represents the company buying the hospice and brought the transfer documents.
cast.account: I stayed in the dining room after 18:15. The trustee had asked to be left alone. I could not have used the service stairs; the contractor had locked the connecting door.
cast.observation: This building is full of old passages. A warm room is hardly evidence of anything. The trust will lose funding if we miss tomorrow’s signature window.
cast.secret: My commission is paid only if the transfer completes. I did not disclose that to the family because I knew how it would sound. It does not make the transfer unlawful.
cast.defense: You can dislike my contract without turning me into the person you need to explain those stairs.
cast.correction: I did leave the dining room briefly to fetch my charger. My folder stayed on the table. I should have said the visit was brief instead of saying I never left.

cast.name: Jules
cast.description: Jules has washed the same saucepan twice. He stayed after the evacuation because he did not want Hana left alone.
cast.relationship: He grew up in the village and has supplied the hospice kitchen for years.
cast.account: I took a tray to the dining room at 18:25. Leonie’s folder was on the table, but her chair was empty. Hana came in ten minutes later and helped me pack supplies.
cast.observation: I heard a wheeled case cross the pantry tiles while I was at the sink. The service passage runs behind that wall. It could have been a trolley; I did not see who was moving it.
cast.secret: I have been taking surplus food home for my father. I used the pantry passage so nobody would see the bags. That is why I kept quiet about hearing wheels there.
cast.defense: Ask me what I heard, and I will tell you. Ask me to turn a sound through a wall into a face, and I cannot.
cast.correction: The chair was empty when I set down the tray. I did not watch it continuously afterward. What I heard behind the pantry wall should remain separate from that one sighting.

cast.name: Omar
cast.description: Omar’s sleeve is marked with red valve grease. He has been trying to finish this repair since Monday.
cast.relationship: Leonie asked him to secure the old wing before the transfer inspection.
cast.account: The connecting door was locked at 17:50. At 18:10 Leonie asked for the key to inspect the meters. I lent it to her and stayed in the plant room until the alarm.
cast.observation: The latch is spring-loaded. It locks behind you unless you turn the small catch. Whoever returned the key would not need it to leave the service passage through Room Four.
cast.secret: I billed for a replacement latch last month and fitted a repaired one. I was afraid the police would assume its failure caused the death. The latch works; my invoice is the lie.
cast.defense: Test the catch with the door open. Do not put someone in that passage to prove what a lock ought to do.
cast.correction: Locking the connecting door did not keep it locked for the whole evening. I lent Leonie the key. My first answer described the job I finished, not every later use of the door.

cast.name: Beth
cast.description: Beth has brought her aunt’s coat, although her aunt is already in the evacuation ambulance. She holds it as if someone will ask for it.
cast.relationship: The amendment removes Beth as sole beneficiary and preserves the hospice as a trust.
cast.account: The trustee told me about the amendment at 18:05. I argued with him. Then I went to the front porch, where Ruth found me after the avalanche warning.
cast.observation: At 18:30 I saw Leonie near the old wing carrying her slim document case. I remember because she told me the dining room was warmer. I thought she was being kind.
cast.secret: I begged my aunt not to change the will. I owe money. She changed it anyway, and I had decided to accept that before you arrived. I cannot prove a decision I made alone.
cast.defense: Ruth saw me crying. That proves I was upset, not that I pushed a man down the stairs.
cast.correction: I recognized Leonie’s slim case, but I did not look at its wheels. The sighting and the tracks are two pieces of information. I should not make them identify one object by themselves.

cast.name: Ruth
cast.description: Ruth keeps a pencil tucked into a sleeve seam. She has never liked signing figures she cannot recalculate.
cast.relationship: She helped the trustee trace the holding company behind the purchase.
cast.account: I found Beth on the porch at 18:22 and stayed with her until the alarm. The access camera is broken; there is no recording of us. We were looking at the snow moving across the road.
cast.observation: The electronic transfer has a different property schedule from the paper copy. A strip of land beside the service road has been added. The trustee had circled that addition in his own draft.
cast.secret: I noticed the company name a month ago and delayed raising it because I wanted the pension settlement signed. I gave myself a deadline. Then somebody died before it arrived.
cast.defense: A beneficiary can be greedy and still be telling the truth about where she stood. Follow the altered schedule as carefully as the argument.
cast.correction: I was with Beth from 18:22 onward. I did not witness her earlier argument. I can account for the later interval without making a claim about everything she had felt before it.

connections.speaker: omar
connections.subject: leonie
connections.text: The returned key puts the passage within your reach, Leonie. Jules’s empty chair leaves a gap in the dining-room alibi. Why say the door made the journey impossible?
connections.reply: I thought the door was locked again. I went to fetch my charger; I did not time the walk.

connections.speaker: hana
connections.subject: leonie
connections.text: Someone used the warm room as a route, not a bedroom. Beth places your case near that route, Leonie. I want its wheels compared before we sign anything.
connections.reply: You would stop a transfer because a relative in debt remembers my luggage. Keep her uncertainty in your notes.

connections.speaker: ruth
connections.subject: beth
connections.text: Beth had a reason to be angry, and she has admitted it. I was with her during the interval we are trying to explain. Her debt does not erase those minutes.
connections.reply: I would rather you remembered the minutes than the things I said on the porch.

timeline: 17:50 Omar locks the connecting door.
18:10 Leonie borrows the key.
18:20 Hana leaves the trustee alive in the office.
18:25 Jules sees Leonie’s empty chair.
18:30 Beth sees Leonie’s case near the old wing; Leonie uses Room Four and the service passage.
18:40 Leonie returns the key after the trustee is killed.
solution: Leonie used the service passage to reach the trustee and recover the amendment. Heating Room Four gave her a plausible reason to direct people away from the cold office wing while keeping her exit comfortable and clear. The key envelope disproves her claim that the door excluded her; the empty chair and the case tracks narrow the interval. Beth’s inheritance dispute was a useful distraction from the altered land schedule.
chapters: An empty bed
The dining-room clock is stopped. You use your own watch and mark which times are remembered, which are written, and which are guesses.
A borrowed key
A plow reaches the lower switchback and turns back. The electronic transfer deadline remains on Leonie’s screen.
The amendment
The old wing cools unevenly. The signed accounts are now more valuable than the keys: they record which doors each person said were closed.
ending_win: The transfer is halted before its signature window. When the patient is told what her amendment cost, she asks whether the staff will still have jobs. The land stays in trust. Nobody finds that an adequate answer to the empty chair.
ending_loss: The transfer completes while the road is still closed. The hospice is described as an unsafe property with defective stairs. The patient’s amendment becomes an unverified intention; the company acquires something more useful than land, which is the authority to empty it.
reconstruction: Leonie was the company’s agent. The transfer contained an altered property schedule that would let a criminal holding company acquire the hospice and the service-road land. The trustee had noticed the alteration; the patient’s amendment would preserve the trust instead. Leonie’s commission depended on completion, but the organization’s loss of the property was the larger motive.

Leonie borrowed Omar’s key at 18:10. After Hana left the trustee alive, she used the service passage, confronted him about the amendment, and pushed him down the office stairs when he would not surrender it. She removed the amendment from his open briefcase. Room Four provided an exit from the passage without crossing the dining room; its turned-up heat made the otherwise empty room look like a place in ordinary use. She returned the key at 18:40.

Jules’s empty-chair sighting makes the dining-room alibi incomplete. Omar’s key loan and the return envelope show the passage remained available. Beth saw the case near the old wing, while the narrow wheel tracks give an independent detail to compare with that sighting. None is a complete account alone; together they explain the journey Leonie said a locked door made impossible.

Beth had argued about the inheritance, but Ruth was with her during the later interval. Jules hid food taken for his father, Omar hid a false repair invoice, and Ruth delayed reporting the company because of her pension settlement. Hana refused an unauthorized copy of the amendment and blamed her own caution afterward. Their motives explain evasions; they do not explain Leonie’s missing journey or the changed land schedule.

interpretation.note: Treat the heated room and wheel tracks as a possible route, not proof of an occupant or a unique bag.

title: The Witness in Carriage Six
setting: A night train stopped between a washed-out bridge and a closed signal
pressure: A witness has been silenced. Someone on the train needs the sealed original to disappear before the police can board.
opening: The train stops without reaching a station. In Carriage Six, a reading lamp shines on an empty cup and a witness who will never reach the hearing. You were escorting him to testify about a freight syndicate. His door is locked, his deposition is missing, and the attendant insists that nobody has crossed the gangway since departure.

A bridge inspection has closed the line ahead. Behind you, floodwater has reached the points. The driver has isolated this section of the train while waiting for help, leaving six people within reach of the witness’s compartment. A courier, an attendant, a retired guard, a doctor, a pianist, and a railway surveyor all have reasons to remember the last stop differently.

You take their written accounts before dividing the watches. The witness’s carbon copy remains in your bag; only you know it is incomplete. Beyond the windows, a signal alternates between red and darkness. Every time it goes dark, someone asks whether the train has started moving.

cast.name: Pavel
cast.description: Pavel has kept his overcoat on. A delivery receipt protrudes from the pocket he keeps touching.
cast.relationship: He was hired to carry the witness’s supplemental papers to the hearing.
cast.account: I stayed on the platform at Bellcross until the guard’s second whistle. Then I entered Carriage Three and remained there until the emergency stop. I never went near Six.
cast.observation: Anyone in this section could have walked along the corridor. My receipt is timed, though. It puts me at the station office while everyone else was settling into their compartments.
cast.secret: I opened the supplemental packet before the journey. A broker paid me to photograph the contents. I told myself it was only commercial information.
cast.defense: A courier’s work is carrying other people’s secrets. Possessing an envelope does not tell you what I did with it.
cast.correction: I used “second whistle” as a familiar expression for departure. I should not have claimed an exact signal. My receipt dates a delivery; it does not prove every minute of my journey.

cast.name: Esme
cast.description: Esme has six brass keys on a chain and a spare pair of shoes under the service seat.
cast.relationship: She checked the witness’s compartment and brought his tea.
cast.account: I served the witness at 22:06, after departure. At 22:10 I saw a grey overcoat disappearing through the service door toward Six. I could not see a face.
cast.observation: The service door sticks unless its handle is lifted first. I heard someone lift it without trying the usual downward turn. That person may have used this train before.
cast.secret: I lent my spare key to Pavel when he said a parcel had been locked in an empty compartment. I got it back before the train stopped. I did not record the loan.
cast.defense: I broke a rule about a key. Do not let me repair that mistake by inventing a face inside a coat.
cast.correction: The grey coat was a movement through the service doorway, not an identification. Lending the spare key is the part I can attach to a named person, and I should have disclosed it first.

cast.name: Dorian
cast.description: Dorian taps his old whistle against a folded timetable but does not blow it. His ticket was bought with a staff discount.
cast.relationship: He trained several of the current crew and keeps correcting their procedures.
cast.account: Bellcross departed on a hand lamp tonight. The guard’s whistle had failed at the previous stop. I stood beside him while he tried it. There was no second whistle.
cast.observation: Pavel said “second whistle” before anyone asked how departure was signalled. It may be a habit of speech. I would compare it with something less dependent on memory.
cast.secret: I let my grandson use my staff travel pass last year. The witness knew and threatened to report it during an argument. That was an ugly quarrel, not a plan.
cast.defense: Railway habit can make a man say the wrong word. It cannot put a hand lamp in one place and a whistle in another.
cast.correction: I know the whistle did not work because I stood beside the guard. I do not know whether Pavel heard another sound and remembered it wrongly. The signal checks his words, not his intentions.

cast.name: Mina
cast.description: Mina’s dinner remains untouched in its paper tray. She introduced herself only after she was asked to examine the witness.
cast.relationship: She treated the witness earlier for travel sickness, with Esme present.
cast.account: I gave him an ordinary travel-sickness tablet before we boarded. Esme saw the packet. When we found him, I asked everyone to leave the cup and bedding where they were.
cast.observation: There is tea spilled on the inside of his cuff and a broken button near the door. I cannot tell you the cause of death here. Those details do not fit a man simply falling asleep undisturbed. The loose pillowcase was bundled under the bed, although Esme says she left it on the pillow.
cast.secret: My registration inquiry is still open after a complaint. I did not want to identify myself as a doctor. If I sound guarded, that is why.
cast.defense: A label on my bag is not a laboratory. We need to preserve what happened in that compartment, not announce a poison because it makes a tidy explanation.
cast.correction: I treated travel sickness before boarding. That does not tell me the cause of his death. The disturbed bedding and broken button are things to preserve, not a diagnosis I can certify here.

cast.name: Luca
cast.description: Luca has put a soft practice keyboard across his knees. He repeats a passage silently when conversations turn toward him.
cast.relationship: His orchestra lost its equipment in a shipment handled by the freight syndicate.
cast.account: I waited outside the station office for a phone signal before departure. The clerk stamped Pavel’s receipt while Pavel was already walking back toward the train. I saw the clerk hand it to the porter.
cast.observation: After departure I heard a parcel tear on the other side of my compartment wall. There was a short argument, then the sound of a case fastening. I could not make out words.
cast.secret: I sold a spare instrument to cover the tour’s wages and told the orchestra it was still in storage. I had hoped the hearing would get us compensation before anyone checked.
cast.defense: I count bars for a living, not train minutes. I remember the order of sounds more confidently than their times.
cast.correction: I saw the clerk give the receipt to the porter. I did not see who finally received it aboard. It breaks a claimed location, but it does not reconstruct the whole corridor journey.

cast.name: Faye
cast.description: Faye’s boots are wrapped in newspaper to keep mud off the seats. She has the bridge inspection plans in a cardboard tube.
cast.relationship: She had warned the railway about the flood risk and expected the witness to support her at the hearing.
cast.account: I was in Three when Pavel claimed to arrive. I remember his empty seat because I wanted somewhere dry for my plans. He came back only after the brakes went on.
cast.observation: The corridor carpet between Five and Six is damp with fine pale grit. Bellcross platform was dry. The grit matches the temporary boards laid outside the service exit at the previous stop; several people used them.
cast.secret: I altered the date on an inspection note after my warning was ignored. I wanted the file to show how early I knew. The danger was real, but the date is false.
cast.defense: Mud can travel on somebody else’s shoes. My note should be checked, and so should the empty seat.
cast.correction: Pavel’s seat was empty while I was in Three, but I was not guarding the doorway. I can identify an interval he did not spend beside me, not every place he could have gone.

clues.text: The service cupboard contains Esme’s spare-key tag. Its loop is newly bent; the key itself opens both the empty parcel compartment and the witness’s door.

connections.speaker: dorian
connections.subject: pavel
connections.text: The whistle does not establish your departure, Pavel, and the porter’s book means the receipt does not establish your location. We need another witness for the interval in Three.
connections.reply: I described an ordinary departure. The words were careless. The delivery still happened.

connections.speaker: esme
connections.subject: pavel
connections.text: I gave you access to that compartment, and Faye did not see you in Three. I cannot identify the coat, but I can stop pretending the key stayed on my chain.
connections.reply: You lent a key without recording it. Are you certain I was the only person who asked?

connections.speaker: mina
connections.subject: faye
connections.text: Faye’s altered inspection date needs investigating, but it does not account for the disturbed compartment. We should not use one discovered lie as a substitute for the missing journey.

timeline: Before departure Mina treats the witness with Esme present.
Bellcross departs by hand lamp, without a working whistle.
The porter carries Pavel’s stamped receipt to Carriage Three.
22:06 Esme serves the witness alive.
22:10 a grey coat uses the service door; Pavel has borrowed the spare key.
Pavel returns to Three after the emergency stop; the witness’s original is missing.
solution: Pavel used the borrowed key to reach the witness and take the original deposition. His platform receipt was stamped in his absence and carried aboard by the porter. The false whistle detail alone could have been a verbal habit; paired with the missing interval in Three and the admitted key loan, it becomes a manufactured journey. His broker served the freight syndicate the witness was about to expose.
chapters: A train without a station
The driver reports that help is coming from the far side of the bridge. The announcement gives no arrival time. You begin with the order of events rather than the clocks.
The borrowed key
The dining-car generator is being rationed. Each time the lights dim, the compartment doors become small black squares along the corridor.
The original and the copy
The flood has stopped rising. Someone asks whether a carbon copy is enough for a court. You ask who knew there were two copies.
ending_win: Police walk along the track carrying their equipment above the water. The deposition leaves in an evidence sleeve instead of a courier’s case. Luca begins his difficult passage again; this time, he lets the keys make a sound.
ending_loss: By the time the train is reached, the original deposition has vanished. The carbon copy supports some charges and none of the names that mattered most. Pavel’s delivery receipt is filed as an ordinary piece of business.
reconstruction: Pavel was the freight syndicate’s agent. He had already sold photographs of the witness’s supplemental papers to a broker. The original deposition would identify the people behind that business, so taking the packet was no longer enough: the witness also had to be prevented from reaching the hearing.

Pavel borrowed Esme’s spare key under the pretext of a parcel locked in an empty compartment. After she served the witness alive at 22:06, he entered Six through the service route, took the deposition, and smothered the witness during the struggle. The spilled tea, broken button, and displaced pillowcase belong to that disturbance. He returned to Three only after the emergency stop.

The receipt was stamped while Pavel was already walking toward the train, then delivered by the porter. It dates paperwork rather than its owner. Dorian’s failed-whistle account exposes the rehearsed departure detail. Faye’s empty-seat interval and Esme’s admitted key loan turn those doubts into a route. The coat sighting supports that route without identifying a face by itself.

Esme concealed a key loan, Mina concealed the inquiry into her registration, and Dorian concealed misuse of his travel pass. Luca had sold an instrument while telling the orchestra it remained in storage. Faye falsified a warning date after her real warning was ignored. Each had a reason to dislike scrutiny. Pavel alone needed the original deposition removed and had supplied a false journey for the interval in which it disappeared.

Place the empty-seat interval beside the last living sighting and service-key access.

interpretation.note: Distinguish a paper timestamp from its owner’s presence and a possible key route from a face identification.

title: What the River Returned
setting: A municipal archive above an evacuated floodplain
pressure: A murdered archivist found proof that a redevelopment company moved a boundary on paper and forced families from land it did not own.
opening: The first thing the river returns is a door. It comes through the archive’s loading entrance with a brass number still screwed to its face: 18. The second thing is a box of records everyone was told had burned. You came to supervise their recovery. The archivist who called you is found dead beside the drying racks before she can show you which page mattered.

Six people have stayed above the evacuation line. They include residents of the demolished street, municipal staff, and the surveyor whose report justified the clearance. The bridge is closed and the rescue crews are working downstream. Someone inside the archive is protecting the company that took the land. The recovered box offers that person one last opportunity to destroy a document nobody expected to see again.

You move the box to the upper reading room and take signed statements before the first watch. Nobody may carry a wet page away alone. Downstairs, the numbered door knocks against a shelving unit whenever the river lifts it. One of the six asks whether you are certain it belonged to a house.

cast.name: Jo
cast.description: Jo wears rubber bands around her sleeves to keep them out of the water. The dead archivist had hired her without asking for references.
cast.relationship: She helped catalogue the recovered box and knows which records were missing before the flood.
cast.account: The archivist opened Box K at 16:10. She sent me upstairs for a drying frame. When I returned, she was arguing quietly with Silas beside the map table.
cast.observation: I had counted twelve folded sheets in Box K. After the alarm there were eleven. I did not read them all, but the missing fold had left a clean rectangle in the mud at the bottom. The square map weight had been moved from that end of the table to the drying rack.
cast.secret: I removed a dismissal letter from my own personnel file last month. The archivist found out and let me replace it without reporting me. I would have done almost anything not to disappoint her again.
cast.defense: Count the folds with me. My mistake in another file does not create the missing sheet in this one.
cast.correction: I counted twelve folds before leaving for the frame. I did not catalogue twelve contents. The missing rectangle shows a sheet was removed; the backing impression is needed to say which boundary it concerned.

cast.name: Tess
cast.description: Tess has a waterline across her trousers and an unopened ration bar in each pocket.
cast.relationship: She brought the first evacuees to the archive and treated the archivist’s injured hand.
cast.account: I bandaged the archivist at 16:00. She had cut her palm on a staple. Later I stayed at the upper entrance, directing people toward the rescue stair.
cast.observation: The fresh bandage is still in the bin by the map table. She took it off to handle something with both hands. I cannot tell you what, or why she did not put it back.
cast.secret: I let my brother take a rescue place intended for a resident whose name was duplicated. I corrected the list afterward. I have been afraid to tell the coordinator.
cast.defense: I can describe a dressing. I cannot date a death from the water on a floor that everyone has crossed.
cast.correction: The discarded dressing establishes that the archivist took it off, not when. My last direct sighting of her alive is the earlier visit. I should keep those two observations apart.

cast.name: Arlan
cast.description: Arlan has brought a key to a shop that no longer exists. He turns it in his pocket while other people talk about parcels.
cast.relationship: His family rented Number 18, the building declared to be an abandoned warehouse.
cast.account: I was at the loading entrance when the door came in. I called Mae to help lift it. We stayed there until Jo shouted for us. That brass 18 came off my shopfront.
cast.observation: The survey calls Number 18 a warehouse with a loading bay on the east side. Our bay was on the west. The only east-side door belonged to the company yard across the lane.
cast.secret: I broke into the redevelopment office last year and took a hard drive. I never found anyone who could read it. I came today hoping the archivist could make use of it.
cast.defense: You can arrest me for the break-in later. First look at which side of the building a family was supposed to have lived on.
cast.correction: The brass number is familiar, but a loose number alone would be poor proof of a building. The west-side loading bay and Ren’s independent drain plan are the checks I can offer.

cast.name: Mae
cast.description: Mae’s emergency badge is upside down. She notices it only after Jo has stared at it for a long time.
cast.relationship: She processed the clearance notices and grew up on the street that was demolished.
cast.account: Arlan and I were downstairs with the door from 16:18. Before that, Silas asked me whether the recovered box included the survey’s field book. I told him to ask the archivist.
cast.observation: The copy used for clearance has the same creased corner on every page, even pages issued on different dates. It looks as if one old sheet supplied the background for several new scans.
cast.secret: I sent the notices after I saw the address discrepancy. My supervisor said the lawyers had checked it. I needed the job and let that sentence end the conversation.
cast.defense: Following an instruction did not make it harmless. But I did not draw the line that made those homes disappear.
cast.correction: I recognized the repeated creased corner after the alarm. Before that I had noticed only the address discrepancy. I should not let a later explanation sound like a warning I acted on earlier.

cast.name: Silas
cast.description: Silas has kept his leather document tube above the water. He calls every room by its official designation.
cast.relationship: His boundary report enabled the purchase of the demolished street.
cast.account: I came only to identify the company’s records. I never opened Box K and had no discussion with the archivist about its contents. My survey was based on a site visit, not an old map.
cast.observation: A door can drift a long way in a flood. The number does not establish where it began. I would not overturn a professional survey on a shopkeeper’s memory.
cast.secret: The company paid an expedited fee that I did not declare in my report. That affects the appearance of independence; it does not by itself change a boundary.
cast.defense: If the line is wrong, show me the original markers. Do not replace one contested document with six contested memories.
cast.correction: I consulted older plans as well as the site. Saying the report came only from a visit was too simple. I still dispute the suggestion that a changed drawing proves a deliberate theft of land.

cast.name: Ren
cast.description: Ren has laid a folded street plan under the rescued kettle. He keeps moving the kettle whenever someone reaches for the plan.
cast.relationship: He mapped the drains before demolition and warned that the clearance would worsen flooding.
cast.account: I was trying to restart the pump near the rear stair. At 16:15 Silas passed me with a damp sleeve and his tube open. I assumed he had been helping with the rescued plans.
cast.observation: My maintenance plan shows Number 18’s west-side drain connection. It was surveyed before the redevelopment report. The east-side connection serves the company yard and has a different pipe diameter.
cast.secret: I approved a cheaper pump after my budget was cut. It was not enough for this flood. I wanted the recovered files to expose the clearance, but I also wanted them to draw attention away from my signature.
cast.defense: The pump failure and the stolen boundary can both be real. One should not be used to wash the other away.
cast.correction: I saw the open tube and damp sleeve. I did not inspect the tube’s contents. The independent drain record is stronger evidence of the original building than my guess about what Silas carried.

clues.title: Ren · Observation
clues.text: My maintenance plan shows Number 18’s west-side drain connection. It was surveyed before the redevelopment report. The east-side connection serves the company yard and has a different pipe diameter.

clues.title: Ren · Private admission
clues.text: I approved a cheaper pump after my budget was cut. It was not enough for this flood. I wanted the recovered files to expose the clearance, but I also wanted them to draw attention away from my signature.

clues.title: The field-book backing sheet
clues.text: Under the map-table blotter is an impression from the missing field-book page. It places the boundary west of Number 18. The surviving clearance copy places it east, leaving the house inside company land.

clues.title: The drying label
clues.text: A paper drying label in the corridor bears “K / 12” and a smear of the same red wax used to seal document tubes. Red sealing wax is also stocked at the archive desk.

connections.speaker: ren
connections.subject: silas
connections.text: An east-side loading bay describes the company yard, not Arlan’s shop. My drain plan gives us a check that predates the dispute. Which building did you actually measure, Silas?
connections.reply: The street was altered before demolition. A service connection can survive a change of use.

connections.speaker: jo
connections.subject: silas
connections.text: You said you never discussed the box. I heard the discussion, and Ren saw you leave with the tube open. The missing page changes the boundary. That is the sequence I need you to explain.
connections.reply: You heard an argument about custody of records. You did not hear its contents, and you did not inspect my tube.

connections.speaker: arlan
connections.subject: mae
connections.text: Mae should have stopped those notices. She has admitted that. But the line was moved before she sent them; letting her take all the blame would leave the person who moved it untouched.
connections.reply: I will identify every notice I processed. Nobody else should have to prove they once lived in their own home.

timeline: Before the clearance, Ren records Number 18’s west-side drain.
16:00 Tess treats the archivist’s hand.
16:10 Box K is opened with twelve folded sheets.
Jo hears Silas arguing with the archivist; Silas removes the original field-book page and kills her.
16:15 Ren sees Silas with a damp sleeve and open tube.
After the alarm Jo counts eleven sheets; the backing impression survives.
solution: Silas’s supposed site survey described the company yard across the lane. Moving its boundary over Number 18 made the clearance appear lawful. The flood returned the original field book, and he killed the archivist to remove it. The crossed accounts of the box and tube establish his opportunity; the independent drain plan and surviving impression explain what the missing page proved. Mae’s compliance helped the fraud without making her the killer.
chapters: Twelve folds
You put dry weights on the recovered papers. The water has made some marks illegible and preserved others that a fire would have erased.
Two sides of a street
A rescue crew reaches the next block. From the reading-room window, the demolished street is visible only as changes in the current.
The line on the map
The box is nearly dry. A document that can be read can also be carried away; you keep the sealed file within reach.
ending_win: The original boundary is entered into the evidence record before the company can claim the box. Arlan asks for the brass number from the floating door. It is not restitution, but he wants to take something home that does not need a lawyer to explain it.
ending_loss: The missing sheet is recorded as flood damage. The clearance remains lawful on paper, which is the only version the company accepts. Downstairs, the numbered door finally comes loose and goes back into the river.
reconstruction: Silas was the redevelopment company’s agent. His report described the yard across the lane as though it were Number 18, moving a boundary so homes could be cleared as company property. Ren’s earlier drain survey and Arlan’s knowledge of the west-side bay supplied independent checks. The flood returned the original field book that the fraud had depended on losing.

At 16:10 the archivist opened Box K with twelve folded sheets. Silas argued with her about the boundary page while Jo fetched a frame. He struck the archivist with the square map weight, moved the weight toward the drying racks, and removed the original page in his document tube. Ren saw him leave with the tube open at 16:15. Jo later counted eleven folds; the backing impression survived the theft.

The missing fold is not itself proof of its contents, and a damp sleeve is not proof of murder. The backing impression identifies the boundary the missing page carried. Jo’s argument, Ren’s departure sighting, and Silas’s denial of discussing the box establish the opportunity he tried to omit. His wrong-side loading bay identifies the false survey beneath the killing.

Mae sent notices after noticing a discrepancy. Ren approved an inadequate pump. Arlan broke into the redevelopment office, Jo removed a letter from her own file, and Tess altered an evacuation allocation for her brother. Their admissions explain genuine wrongdoing around the disaster. None redraws the original boundary or accounts for the page taken from the archivist.

timing.note: Order the opening, argument, departure with an open tube, and later missing fold.

interpretation.note: Identify the surveyed building through independent bay and drain orientation, rather than a drifting house number.
Use the backing impression to identify a missing sheet’s boundary content, rather than inferring content from a count.

incidents.night: {name} is found dead before the archive watch returns upstairs. Below the reading room, the numbered door knocks against the shelving again. You keep the witness’s sealed notes above the flood line with the survey; no drying rack can restore an answer that was never recorded.
incidents.vote: {name} is placed under guard away from the recovered records. The drying frames and survey stay under shared watch. Their account remains in the file, with its limits intact.
incidents.rescue: {name} survives the attack and returns above the flood line. A clear place is made between the drying frames for the watch to regroup. The records remain together, and the protector remains unnamed.

leads.text: The surviving impression and the independent drain plan are both in the file. Read their boundaries together before trusting a familiar address.

title: The Last Dress Rehearsal
setting: A condemned theatre during its final benefit performance
pressure: A stage manager has found that the charity benefit is financing a criminal front. The last rehearsal has become a closed inquiry.
opening: The curtain rises on an empty chair. It is the wrong cue, and the actors laugh until the work lights find the stage manager beneath the scenery bridge. You came because she asked you to inspect the benefit’s accounts after the rehearsal. Her note said: Don’t let them explain it as a mistake in the books.

A storm has brought a facade down across the alley. The fire crew has shut the street and told the six remaining company members to wait in the reinforced rehearsal wing. One of them is using the theatre’s charity appeal to move money for a criminal organization. The stage manager had prepared a second set of accounts. They have disappeared from her prompt desk.

You take statements under the work lights and lock the prompt desk before the first watch. Everyone knows how to make darkness here, and almost everyone knows how to move through it. On the empty chair, somebody has left the small brass bell that calls the actors back from an interval.

cast.name: Clio
cast.description: Clio has the running order pinned to her sleeve. She keeps reaching to call a cue that will never be taken.
cast.relationship: She shared the prompt desk with the victim and expected to take over next season.
cast.account: I called the blackout at 19:32 from the prompt corner. The curtain rose before I gave the next cue. I went to the work-light switch as soon as I saw it moving.
cast.observation: The cue lamp on the scenery bridge had been unplugged. From the fly gallery, you could see the stage go dark but not receive my permission to move anything.
cast.secret: I had copied the victim’s contact list before applying for her job elsewhere. She found the copy. We argued, and I was afraid she would refuse me a reference.
cast.defense: I called a blackout, not a movement on the bridge. The running order shows the difference even if nobody heard my voice.
cast.correction: I called the blackout and then held the bridge. I did not see who touched the curtain control. My running order can establish the intended sequence, not every action that interrupted it.

cast.name: Ben
cast.description: Ben has a strip of white tape wrapped around his thumb. He has worked the same ropes for thirty years.
cast.relationship: He operated the scenery bridge and taught Vera the emergency release during inspections.
cast.account: I locked the bridge brake before the blackout and went to the wings. Vera said she would check the donor banner upstairs. I did not see her come back down.
cast.observation: The brake’s locking pin was on the gallery floor afterward. It has to be lifted out by hand. A lost cue can explain timing; it cannot remove that pin.
cast.secret: The pin is a replacement I made myself because the theatre would not buy the approved part. It fits. I knew the paperwork would make me look responsible before anyone tested it.
cast.defense: I will put my work on the table. A bad maintenance record is not a hand pulling a pin during a blackout.
cast.correction: I tested the pin before leaving the gallery. I did not watch it afterward. The hand action needed to remove it matters more than my assumption that nobody would touch it.

cast.name: Vera
cast.description: Vera has a donor’s ribbon fixed to her coat and several missed calls on her phone. She turns the phone face down before speaking.
cast.relationship: She controls the benefit accounts and negotiated the theatre’s final lease extension.
cast.account: I was in the foyer throughout the blackout, speaking to a donor. I heard Clio call the bridge cue and assumed the movement was intended. I never went above the stage.
cast.observation: The theatre has been closing for ten years. Every repair is improvised. I would start with the equipment before deciding that somebody here wanted this.
cast.secret: I moved money between the benefit account and my production account to cover wages. I planned to replace it after the performance. The books look worse than the situation was.
cast.defense: I kept this company paid when everyone else was ready to walk away. That is not an answer to every question, but it is part of the account.
cast.correction: I may have heard the curtain motor and taken it for a movement cue. I should not have quoted Clio’s instruction as though I remembered its words. That was an inference I stated as a memory.

cast.name: Rafi
cast.description: Rafi has removed only half his stage makeup. A dark line divides the face he shows the room.
cast.relationship: He helped the victim document safety concerns and was first to reach her.
cast.account: I waited behind the closed fire door during the blackout. From there, I could not hear words from the prompt corner. I heard the curtain motor and came through when Clio switched on the work lights.
cast.observation: The foyer speaker was disconnected before the rehearsal because it hummed. I helped unplug it. Anyone in the foyer could hear the building, but not Clio’s cue over the monitor.
cast.secret: I had agreed to speak publicly about the unsafe bridge after the show. Then Vera offered the company another season and I withdrew. The victim had stopped trusting me.
cast.defense: I know what silence sounded like behind that door. I cannot tell you what somebody heard from a place I was not standing.
cast.correction: The closed fire door muffled the prompt corner; it did not make the whole building silent. I can explain why the words were hard to hear, not decide what another person thought they heard.

cast.name: Una
cast.description: Una’s measuring tape is knotted at one end. She has been quietly mending clothes that will be sold with the building.
cast.relationship: She found invoices that did not match the costumes purchased for the benefit.
cast.account: I took a spare ribbon to Vera before the blackout. She was at the stair to the fly gallery, not in the foyer. She told me the donor wanted the banner moved.
cast.observation: After the alarm, the ribbon on Vera’s coat was torn at its lower edge. I had cut it square. It could have snagged anywhere, but there is a small matching strip beside the gallery brake.
cast.secret: I inflated a costume invoice to pay an assistant whose wages were overdue. The victim noticed and asked me to correct it. I had not done so when she died.
cast.defense: Cloth catches on ordinary things. Compare the stair sighting with the ribbon; do not ask the ribbon to stand alone.
cast.correction: I saw Vera at the gallery stair before the blackout. I did not follow her up it. The torn ribbon gives a detail to compare, but it does not turn me into a witness to the release.

cast.name: Milo
cast.description: Milo holds the console password on a paper scrap because he still does not trust himself to remember it.
cast.relationship: The victim persuaded the theatre to hire him despite his lack of formal training.
cast.account: The console records a blackout at 19:32 and work lights at 19:34. The bridge is mechanical and does not appear in the lighting log. I stayed at the console.
cast.observation: The prompt microphone was working; Clio’s voice is on the rehearsal recording. She says “hold the bridge” after the blackout. She never calls it to move.
cast.secret: I deleted a failed lighting cue from an earlier rehearsal to keep the senior operator from blaming me. Tonight’s file is still intact. I made a copy before anyone asked.
cast.defense: A lighting log does not record every action in a theatre. It can still show which action was actually called.
cast.correction: The audio preserves Clio’s words; my console file preserves lighting changes. Neither records a hand removing a mechanical pin. We need both records without treating either as a camera.

connections.speaker: clio
connections.subject: vera
connections.text: You remembered hearing a bridge cue from a foyer with no monitor. The recording says the opposite. Did you hear me from somewhere closer to the stage?
connections.reply: I heard somebody call. In the dark I assumed it was you. I will not pretend to recall every word now.

connections.speaker: ben
connections.subject: vera
connections.text: I left the brake pinned and saw you take the gallery stair. Una places you there too. The missing pin is an action somebody took, not a cue somebody misunderstood.
connections.reply: You left a homemade safety part in a condemned theatre. You have as much reason as anyone to want this to be deliberate.

connections.speaker: milo
connections.subject: una
connections.text: Una’s false invoice paid one person whose work we can check. These other transfers went to three company names at one address. Both are wrong; they are not the same trail.
connections.reply: I will bring the assistant’s payment record. I should not have hidden a wage inside a costume bill.

timeline: Before rehearsal Rafi disconnects the humming foyer monitor.
Ben locks the bridge brake and sees Vera take the gallery stair.
Una sees Vera at the stair before the blackout.
19:32 Clio calls blackout, then orders the bridge held.
Vera removes the brake pin and kills the stage manager; the early curtain movement exposes the aftermath.
19:34 Clio calls work lights; Milo preserves the rehearsal file.
solution: Vera killed the stage manager to stop the benefit accounts reaching you. Her explanation relied on a cue that was never called and could not have been heard from the foyer. Ben and Una place her on the gallery route; the removed brake pin shows a deliberate act. The homemade part and Una’s false invoice supplied believable distractions, but neither explains Vera’s invented cue or the payments she authorized. Reaching for the gallery work light afterward, she used the curtain control and exposed the scene sooner than she intended.
chapters: Under work lights
Without the stage lighting, the painted walls look thin. You ask everyone to separate what they saw from what they were waiting to be told.
Hold the bridge
Rain runs through the blocked alley. The company has spent years trusting cues from people it could not see; tonight that habit needs examining.
After the curtain
The emergency crew tests the street below. Inside, the benefit accounts and the rehearsal track wait on the same table.
ending_win: The benefit is cancelled, and the theatre’s last recorded instruction is to hold the bridge. The company submits the accounts together. Nobody agrees on whether the building could have been saved, but the death is no longer filed among its maintenance defects.
ending_loss: The death is attributed to an improvised brake and a misunderstood cue. The donor companies recover their contributions before the accounts are seized. When the theatre is emptied, the prompt desk goes first.
reconstruction: Vera was the organization’s agent. The benefit’s donations were passing through companies with a shared return address. The stage manager had preserved a second account of those transfers and had asked for an independent review. Vera’s attempts to keep the company paid also gave her an explanation for moving money that she hoped nobody would examine too closely.

Vera went to the gallery while claiming she remained in the foyer. During the blackout she lifted the bridge’s locking pin by hand and released the suspended scenery while the stage manager was beneath it. Reaching for the gallery work light afterward, she operated the curtain control and exposed the scene sooner than she intended. She then treated the death as a misunderstood cue and defective maintenance.

Clio called for the bridge to be held, not released. Milo preserved that instruction on the rehearsal audio. Rafi had helped disconnect the foyer monitor, so Vera’s account of hearing the invented cue from there did not establish the location she claimed. Ben and Una place her on the gallery route; the missing pin distinguishes an action from a mistaken instruction.

Ben had fitted an undocumented replacement part. Una inflated an invoice to pay an assistant, Clio copied a contact list while applying elsewhere, and Milo deleted an earlier failed cue. Rafi withdrew a safety complaint when another season was offered. These compromises explain why the company hesitated to speak. They do not explain the manually removed pin, Vera’s false location, or the benefit transfers she authorized.

Order the pinned brake, gallery approach, and manually removed pin around the blackout.

title: The Winter Seed
setting: A remote seed repository during a prolonged power failure
pressure: A quality auditor discovered that relief seed had been substituted before shipment. The reference sample is now the only local check on her finding.
opening: The cold-room alarm has been sounding so long that nobody notices when it stops. The quality auditor is found dead in the preparation room, beside a tray of seeds laid out as carefully as coins. You came to witness the sealing of her reference sample. Its label is intact, but the packet under it feels wrong in your hand.

A landslide has cut the road to the repository. The backup generator can hold one room cold, and six staff and visitors are arguing over which collection should be saved. One of them represents the people who substituted cheap seed for a relief shipment. If the reference sample is lost, villages far from this mountain will have only a failed harvest to prove what they were sent.

You ask for signed accounts before organizing watches, and keep the sample in the preparation room where everyone can see the seal. The tray on the auditor’s desk contains two sizes of seed. An argument begins about whether anyone without a microscope has a right to notice that.

cast.name: Anika
cast.description: Anika has marked the threatened collections on a wall chart in green pencil. She will not mark any of them as expendable.
cast.relationship: She helped the auditor select the reference sample and insists on retaining its original envelope.
cast.account: We sealed the sample at 14:10 in a narrow kraft envelope. The auditor kept it on the preparation bench. I went to choose collections for the generator circuit at 14:20.
cast.observation: The envelope now under the label is wider and has a blue seam. Our reference envelopes have brown seams. Packaging changed; that does not by itself tell us whether the contents changed with it.
cast.secret: I kept an unauthorized duplicate of a rare collection in my office. If the power failed, I wanted something to survive outside the approved plan. I was afraid an inspection would destroy it.
cast.defense: We can document two envelopes without pretending we have already proved two species. Preserve the difference first.
cast.correction: I identified our narrow envelope when we sealed it. The blue seam shows a packaging change later, not a species identification. The contents still need an independent test.

cast.name: Leila
cast.description: Leila has taped handwritten instructions to the generator-room first-aid cabinet. She dislikes being asked to certify more than she has seen.
cast.relationship: She was accompanying a visiting relief delegation and treated the auditor for exhaustion.
cast.account: I saw the auditor alive at 14:25. She asked whether the road crew could carry a small sealed packet down on foot. I went to the radio room to ask.
cast.observation: The preparation-room latch can be held open with a flat card. A blue plastic dispatch card was on the floor when we found her. I left it where it was. A transport-satchel strap lay beside her chair with one end pulled from its buckle. I left that there as well.
cast.secret: I told the relief delegation their seed was probably safe before the testing was complete. They needed something hopeful to report. I had no result that justified my confidence.
cast.defense: I will not give you another reassuring answer before the evidence exists. That includes an answer about who killed her.
cast.correction: The dispatch card could hold the latch open. I did not see it being used that way. I should give you the object’s position and leave the missing action as a question.

cast.name: Cass
cast.description: Cass has written the fuel level on the back of one hand. He rubs the figure away and writes it again after every reading.
cast.relationship: He is responsible for the only power source still working.
cast.account: Soren signed into the generator room at 14:20. He left before I completed the fuel check. I remained there until 14:45. A signature does not mean we spent the interval together.
cast.observation: The generator inspection sheet has only an arrival column. The auditor had pointed that out last week when a delivery driver used it to claim an hour on site.
cast.secret: I siphoned reserve fuel into my own vehicle before the storm warning. I put most of it back. The generator shortage is partly mine, and I knew you would find that out.
cast.defense: My fuel theft can be measured. It cannot lengthen the time Soren stood beside me.
cast.correction: I can give the order of my fuel checks more confidently than the exact minute Soren left. He was gone before I completed the first one; my signature does not make us continuous witnesses for each other.

cast.name: Dara
cast.description: Dara has brought a handful of seed saved from her village’s last planting. She keeps it in a cloth bag, separate from every official sample.
cast.relationship: She asked for the audit after farmers reported that the delivered seed looked unfamiliar.
cast.account: I waited outside the preparation room after lunch. At 14:32 Soren came out carrying a flat blue-edged packet. He said the auditor had sent him for a transport label.
cast.observation: My village’s delivery used packets with blue seams. I cannot identify a batch by color alone. I can say the packet he carried looked like the delivery stock, not the little envelope Anika had shown me.
cast.secret: I exaggerated the number of families already affected because the first complaint was ignored. The figures need correcting. The seeds in my bag do not.
cast.defense: I am not asking you to trust a color over a test. I am asking you not to ignore a color because a test takes longer.
cast.correction: I recognized the blue-seamed delivery stock, not a unique packet. My sighting puts a kind of envelope in Soren’s hands. The duplicate label and dispatch record must do the identifying.

cast.name: Niko
cast.description: Niko has arranged the unused sample labels by number. He starts over whenever someone moves the desk.
cast.relationship: He logged the auditor’s batches and was supposed to accompany the reference to the laboratory.
cast.account: The auditor asked me to print a duplicate label at 14:05. She wanted the number readable even if the first label got wet. Soren collected the spare from my desk while I was at the printer.
cast.observation: I found the duplicate backing paper in the dispatch bin after the alarm. The label number matches the reference. A copied number can make a different packet appear continuous in the log.
cast.secret: I entered two batch results before the tests finished because the dispatch deadline was approaching. They were estimates. The auditor was going to make me correct them in front of the whole team.
cast.defense: The wrong entries are mine. A duplicate label leaving my desk is a separate event, and I should have stopped it.
cast.correction: The spare label was intended to preserve a number, not authorize a replacement packet. I should have said that distinction when Soren collected it. Printing a duplicate did not give him the auditor’s approval.

cast.name: Soren
cast.description: Soren has a polished pen and a keycard on a visitor’s lanyard. He keeps offering to take the paperwork off other people’s hands.
cast.relationship: He negotiated the relief purchase and manages the supplier’s dispute with the repository.
cast.account: I was with Cass from 14:20 until 14:45. The inspection sheet confirms it. I did not enter the preparation room after the sample was sealed.
cast.observation: Packets are replaced when seals get wet. That is ordinary logistics, not necessarily substitution. The laboratory result will be more useful than an argument about stationery.
cast.secret: The supplier paid for my travel and accommodation. I should have declared that before advising on the complaint. I still believe the original contract was defensible.
cast.defense: A chain of custody can be messy without being criminal. You need to prove the contents changed, not merely that someone touched a label.
cast.correction: I stepped out to arrange transport. Using Cass’s inspection interval for my whole stay was inaccurate. I still say that handling a reference packet is not proof of changing its contents.
